name: Portopulmonary hypertension
aliases: pulmonary arterial hypertension associated with portal hypertension

reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AASLD
clinicalPearls: Defined as pulmonary arterial hypertension developing in a patient with portal hypertension, in the absence of another explanation for the raised pulmonary pressures
It reflects true elevation of pulmonary vascular resistance from arterial remodelling, in contrast to the vasodilatation of hepatopulmonary syndrome
Presents with exertional dyspnoea, fatigue, and, in advanced disease, signs of right heart strain such as a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound, peripheral oedema, and syncope
Doppler echocardiography is the principal screening tool, with right heart catheterisation required to confirm the diagnosis and quantify pulmonary pressures and resistance

Diagnosis rests on demonstrating raised mean pulmonary artery pressure with elevated pulmonary vascular resistance and a normal or low pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, distinguishing it from volume overload
Severity of pulmonary hypertension does not correlate with the degree of liver dysfunction and can occur with relatively preserved liver function
Moderate to severe disease markedly increases the risk of liver transplantation and may contraindicate it until pulmonary pressures are medically controlled
Pulmonary vasodilator therapy directed at the pulmonary arterial hypertension can lower pressures and improve transplant candidacy in selected patients
reference.pathophysiology: Portopulmonary hypertension arises when portal hypertension leads to progressive remodelling and increased resistance of the pulmonary arterial bed. Portosystemic shunting is thought to expose the pulmonary circulation to vasoactive and proliferative mediators normally cleared by the liver, together with high pulmonary blood flow and shear stress, driving endothelial dysfunction, smooth muscle proliferation, in situ thrombosis, and plexiform vascular lesions similar to those of idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension. The consequent rise in pulmonary vascular resistance increases right ventricular afterload, ultimately causing right ventricular hypertrophy, dilatation, and failure. Because the primary abnormality is vasoconstriction and vascular remodelling rather than the vasodilatation of hepatopulmonary syndrome, the two conditions are physiologically opposite despite sharing a portal hypertensive background.
additionalDifferentials: Volume overload with elevated left-sided filling pressures
Left heart disease causing pulmonary hypertension
Pulmonary hypertension from chronic lung disease
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic Doppler echocardiography to estimate pulmonary pressures and assess right ventricular function
Right heart catheterisation to confirm elevated mean pulmonary artery pressure and pulmonary vascular resistance with a normal wedge pressure
Assessment to exclude other causes of pulmonary hypertension, including thromboembolic and left heart disease
Evaluation of right ventricular size and function
Functional assessment such as exercise capacity testing
Staging of the underlying liver disease and portal hypertension
redFlags: Syncope or presyncope indicating severe pulmonary hypertension and critical right ventricular compromise
Signs of decompensated right heart failure
Severely elevated pulmonary pressures that contraindicate transplantation until controlled
Rapidly progressive exertional dyspnoea and hypoxaemia
reference.prognosis: Untreated moderate to severe portopulmonary hypertension carries a poor prognosis owing to progressive right heart failure; targeted pulmonary vasodilator therapy can lower pulmonary pressures and, in selected patients, restore eligibility for liver transplantation, which offers the potential for improvement, whereas severe uncontrolled disease markedly increases peri-transplant mortality.
pitfalls: Confusing it with hepatopulmonary syndrome, leading to inappropriate management
Attributing raised pulmonary pressures on echocardiography to fluid overload without confirmatory catheterisation
Proceeding to liver transplantation without recognising severe pulmonary hypertension and its high operative risk
Assuming pulmonary hypertension severity mirrors the severity of liver disease
